summary:
Jesse, a three-year Figma software engineer, explains how Figma's first MCP server was built in roughly three months as an unofficial 20%-style side project after seeing an internal demo of Anthropic's MCP spec. Targeting developers as the earliest adopters, the small 'MCPeeps' team shipped a local plugin-based server that let a single prompt pull component data, spacing, and variables into a coding agent.

Figma's C++ scene graph (similar to the HTML DOM) could be represented three ways: an abstract internal JSX-like format, a React+Tailwind representation inherited from Figma's sites product, or inline images. They chose React+Tailwind on a hunch that models had been trained on the most of that markup; output today is pixel perfect. Inline base64 images blew up the context window, so images are now supplementary rather than embedded.

Pixel-perfect output isn't enough for enterprises that want their own accessible, internationalized components, so Code Connect was wired into the MCP server to return a pointer to the user's real component instead of generated markup. Two hours grading one eval in an Excel spreadsheet led to automated LLM-judge evals running hundreds of times per week.

When elicitation and sampling weren't supported by clients, the team hacked around them with prompts and tool calls: asking the user permission to map an unlinked component, having the agent scan code for matches, and adding optional query arguments so agents could self-report their language and framework. They shipped local first via an IPC bridge inside Figma's Electron desktop app to a node process running a server-sent-events endpoint, and launched the remote streamable HTTP server in September 2025, with both servers reaching GA in October 2025 and read/write capabilities added thereafter, making it one of Figma's fastest-growing products.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: A 20% project at a company without 20% projects
sections.summary: Jesse introduces himself as a three-year Figma software engineer and frames the talk around building Figma's first MCP server in about three months. He sets the scene in November 2024 when Anthropic released the MCP spec and only Anthropic's own clients supported it. After seeing an internal demo in Cursor, he pitched an unofficial 20%-style side project (one day a week) so non-designers could use Figma, got staffed with a small 'MCPeeps' team, and started building. A few weeks into architecture work, a new spec version deprecated the server-sent events transport they had chosen, and clients were adding MCP features at uneven paces. VS Code didn't reach GA until July, and even then not all features were implemented; only tools were widely supported. They kept building anyway.

sections.title: What the local server gave developers
sections.summary: Jesse recaps that about a year ago they launched the local MCP server, heavily designed for developer use cases. A single prompt like 'help me implement this' let a developer pull what they'd normally get from Figma's dev mode—component data, spacing, variables—into their coding agent. They kept adding more tools for FigJam, Make, and others, all sharing the goal of making Figma context available to developers wherever they are.

sections.title: Three ways to represent a scene graph
sections.summary: Jesse explains that Figma's canvas is a C++ scene graph, a graph of connected nodes not unlike the HTML DOM. They considered three representations: an internal JSX/XML-like format that was abstract and sparse but lacked rigorous fidelity, a React+Tailwind representation (D2R) inherited from Figma's sites product that converts the scene graph into HTML, and plain images. They chose React+Tailwind on a hunch that models had been trained on the most of that markup, and current output is pixel perfect. They considered images insufficient on their own because early-2025 agents weren't great at converting images directly to HTML/CSS, so images were used as additional context alongside code.

sections.title: Why images alone did not work
sections.summary: Images within the scene graph are abstracted to the top level. Their first attempt at passing base64 data inline was a terrible idea that blew up the context window. Now they also pass an image of the current node to the agent as supplementary context; while the image alone does not convert well to code, code plus image yields better agentic output.

sections.title: Grading evals by hand, once
sections.summary: Jesse describes how the team measured quality. Their first evals mixed quantitative checks (did it use the right variables, theming, and spacing) with qualitative ones (did it look good, did it make good decisions with incomplete information). They spent about two hours grading one eval in an Excel spreadsheet and swore never to do it again. They built toy repos, coded up a web app to streamline grading, and noted the lack of open-source code paired with Figma files forced them to create their own test fixtures. Today, evals run hundreds of times per week behind LLM judges, letting engineers grade prompt changes without a human in the loop.

sections.title: Code Connect, and why pixel perfect is not enough
sections.summary: Pixel-perfect React+Tailwind output is only half the story: enterprises care about using their own accessible, internationalized components, not a beautiful generated button. Figma's existing Code Connect, which links design components to components in a codebase, was wired into the MCP server so the agent receives a pointer to the user's real component instead of a verbose generated block. The example shown converts a large React+Tailwind button into a minimal 'use button component' call, dramatically reducing context size.

sections.title: Elicitation and sampling, and hacking around them
sections.summary: After settling the serialization syntax, the team looked at what else the MCP spec could do. Many features were experimental or unimplemented, captured in their March 2025 client compatibility matrix. They exposed resources (e.g., help articles) so agents could figure out how to use the server instead of erroring. Server instructions weren't implemented by any client until Anthropic highlighted them, so they bolted instructions onto each tool call. They wanted elicitation (asking the user a structured question) combined with sampling (server querying the client's LLM, since deprecated) so they could ask the user to map their codebase for Code Connect and reduce output context. Most clients didn't implement these features, and even VS Code's sampling could only query a general agent, not one scoped to the codebase.

sections.title: Hacking around elicitation and sampling with prompts and tools
sections.summary: Because elicitation and sampling were largely unimplemented, the team mimicked them using prompts and tool calls. When fetching context for a component that wasn't code connected, they would send down a prompt asking the user for permission to map the unlinked component (mimicking elicitation), then a second prompt asking the agent to scan the user's code for potential matches (mimicking sampling). The agent returns suggestions in a specified format in bulk, and the team creates many code connections at once. Jesse recommends the MCP inspector as an open-source debugging tool. To gauge whether React+Tailwind worked for non-React codebases, they added optional query arguments to tool calls like get_design_context so agents could self-report their language and framework. The signal is imperfect because 'agents lie,' but it revealed which user types had a worse experience and pointed to translation-layer problems.

sections.title: Shipping local first, then remote
sections.summary: While working toward the first beta, the team targeted four goals: launch quickly, maintain a high security bar, respect file permissions, and respect pricing/packaging to avoid abuse vectors. After the spec introduced OAuth in March 2025, they chose to keep the server local because until HMAR (likely a typo for streamable HTTP) there was no auth spec to build from and they could reuse infrastructure: the Figma desktop app is Electron, runs figma.com as its front end, and uses an IPC bridge to a node process that talks to the file system. They exposed a server-sent-events endpoint in node so clients could talk directly locally. Enterprises liked that data stayed local, and this was the fastest path to product-market fit. They launched internally to honest feedback, then began working on the remote server immediately.

sections.title: How early all of this still is
sections.summary: The remote server launched in September 2025 and both servers reached GA in October 2025. Adding read/write capabilities made the MCP server one of Figma's fastest-growing products, which the team did not expect. Jesse pivoted to a related product called 'Make in your local codebase' after seeing research that designers wanted to write production code in some cases; it became Figma's agent solution for git/GitHub and local codebases. He closes with two takeaways: the MCP spec is only about two years old and best practices are still emerging, and Figma gives engineers leeway to build and run with new products—he wasn't staffed on MCP or Make but helped build both.
